verses.translation_literal: A song of the ascents. Much [= many times] they have hemmed me in from my youth, let Israel say, please:
verses.translation_dramatic: A song for the climb up to the mountain. Again and again they have pressed in on me, ever since I was young. Let Israel say it. Let Israel say it now, aloud:
verses.directors_commentary:
This is one of the fifteen Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120-134), and the 'I' that speaks is the whole people. Radak reads the 'youth' as the beginning of the nation's exile; Malbim reads it as the time Israel became a nation, when the peoples around it first rose up to destroy it. The voice is a leader giving a cue and the people answering, so stage it as a call-and-response: the cantor sets the line, and 'let Israel say, please' (יֹאמַר־נָא) is an invitation to the crowd to take the next breath with him. The 'please' is a particle of polite urging, which the KJV turns into 'now', and which has the force of 'come on, say it'.

The KJV 'Many a time have they afflicted me' is sound but gentle. The verb צָרַר means to bind, constrict, hem in, and its participle is the ordinary Hebrew word for an enemy (צַר, 'one who presses you'). The image is of an enemy who squeezes. The KJV also carries the title as a separate verse (129:0) and calls it a song of 'degrees', which is the Latin gradus, 'steps'; the Hebrew מַעֲלוֹת is 'ascents', from עלה 'go up', and refers to the climb to Jerusalem.

philological_notes.note: 'The ascents', the title of Psalms 120-134. Traditionally it means the pilgrim climb up to Jerusalem for the festivals, or the steps of the Temple. The KJV's 'degrees' is a Latin loan (gradus 'step').
Feminine of 'much', used as an adverb: 'many times, often'. 'Times' is unsaid in the Hebrew and bracketed in the literal layer.
From צרר 'bind, press, be hostile'. The noun for an enemy (צַר) comes from the same root, so the line says: the pressers have pressed me.

verses.translation_literal: Much [= many times] they have hemmed me in from my youth, also they have not been able to me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Again and again they have pressed in on me, ever since I was young. And yet they have never had their way with me. Never once have they won.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first half of the line is repeated word for word from verse 1, so the crowd sings it back: this is the 'refrain' that Radak says Hebrew repeats to strengthen the thanks to God. The turn comes in the second half, with גַּם לֹא, 'yet not', where the voice drops from complaint to defiance. Do not play it as bragging. The people who say it have the scars, and the line is a statement of fact about survival, made in the same breath as the suffering.

The KJV 'yet they have not prevailed against me' is a fair rendering, though 'against' is an English addition: the Hebrew has only יָכְלוּ לִי, 'they were not able to me', an idiom for 'got the better of me'. Meiri and Metzudat David both read it as 'could not finish me off', which is why the ancient listeners would hear survival as the point, not victory.

philological_notes.note: 'They were able to me', i.e. they had the power over me, they overcame me. The verb needs no object; the preposition 'to me' marks the one over whom the power was exercised. Metzudat David reads 'to make an end of me'.

verses.translation_literal: Upon my back plowers have plowed, they have made long their furrows.
verses.translation_dramatic: They ploughed across my back as if I were a field. Ploughmen drove their blades down the length of me, and made the furrows long.
verses.directors_commentary:
The image is a farm, and every listener had one in their own memory: the wooden plough pulled by a pair of oxen, with the ploughman leaning on a single stilt, and the furrow cut as long as the animals could pull without stopping. Meiri and Radak explain the length of the furrow (מַעֲנָה): the ploughman measures a line by the strength of the oxen, and the oxen have no rest until they reach the end of it. To 'make long the furrow' is therefore to give the victim no rest, in the way that the tradition reads it.

The verse is about a people laid out flat, a back turned into earth. The KJV 'plowers plowed upon my back' is accurate; the Hebrew plays on the root חרש, which gives a noun and a verb side by side (חָרְשׁוּ חֹרְשִׁים, 'plowed the plowers'), and English can keep it with 'plowers plowed'. BBE's 'the wounds they made' is not in the Hebrew: it explains the image instead of saying it. Hold to the farm, and let the audience see the wound without being told.

philological_notes.note: A figura etymologica: the verb and its participle from the same root. Keep it in English as 'plowers plowed'. The verb חרש 'to plow' is a homograph of another root 'to devise (evil)', and the ear may catch both meanings.

'Their furrows', the long cut line of the plow. The word occurs only here and in 1 Samuel 14:14 ('half a furrow of a field'). Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak explain it as the furrow line. The written text (Ketiv) and the reading tradition (Qere) differ in the pointing; the sense is the same.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH [is] righteous, he has cut the cord of the wicked.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the LORD is righteous. The LORD has cut the cords, the cords that bound the wicked to the plough, and the plough stands still in the furrow.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood changes in three words: 'YHWH is righteous' (יְהוָה צַדִּיק) is the whole turn of the psalm. The singers go from what was done to them to what was done for them, and the verb is in the perfect, 'he has cut', stated as a fact already true. Radak and Meiri hear it as a prophetic perfect, the future spoken as done, and the KJV 'hath cut asunder' keeps the past; both readings are possible and the stage direction is the same, the sharp downstroke on the verb, with the cord falling.

The 'cord' (עֲבוֹת) is a thick twisted rope, the kind used to harness a team to a yoke. That keeps the farm image alive: the oxen, now the wicked's own, are loosed from the plough by God cutting the harness. Radak says it means the cords of the yoke, and Malbim, who follows the plough through, says that the oxen cannot be driven. The KJV 'cords' is right; its plural over-translates a singular collective, 'the rope of the wicked'. The KJV also has 'The Lord' in capitals for the divine name; the Hebrew has the tetragrammaton, YHWH, and here it is the point.

philological_notes.note: A twisted cord or rope, thick enough to tie an animal or a bound prisoner (Judges 15:13-14, Psalm 118:27). In this plough image it is the harness cord. The word appears as a collective singular construct.
Piel 'cut off, cut through'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as cutting and severing, citing the cutting of gold into threads in Exodus 39:3. The Piel carries the sense of a decisive severance.

verses.translation_literal: Let them be ashamed and turned back, backward, all [who] hate Zion.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them be ashamed. Let them turn on their heels and go back the way they came: every one of them who hated Zion.
verses.directors_commentary:
From here the psalm goes from statement to wish. Two jussive verbs, יֵבֹשׁוּ and יִסֹּגוּ, open the line without a subject; the subject, 'all who hate Zion', is held to the end, which is a way to build the sentence so that the curse falls on the last word. Perform it as a prayer, not a threat: the singers ask for the haters' reversal, not their death.

The KJV 'confounded' is an archaism (to be put to confusion) that now sounds like 'puzzled'. The Hebrew בּוֹשׁ is 'to be put to shame', a public loss of face in an honour culture. 'Turned back' (סוּג) is the posture of the beaten, retreating with their faces to the field, as Metzudat David says: it is the manner of one ashamed to go back the way he came. 'Zion' is the Temple hill and the city, and also, in Ibn Ezra's gloss, the assembly of Israel; Radak says the nations do not hate the place but its people. The YLT drops the jussive and reads an indicative, 'confounded and turn backward do all hating Zion'. I follow the optative of KJV, ASV and BBE.

philological_notes.note: A Niphal of סוג, 'be turned back, retreat', with 'backward' repeating the idea. A standard phrase for a retreat in defeat. Metzudat Zion compares it to 'we have not turned back' (2 Samuel 1:22).
Zion: the hill of Jerusalem, and by extension the city and its people. Ibn Ezra reads it as the assembly of Israel; Radak says the hatred is of Zion's sons.

token_glosses.gloss: and let them be turned back

verses.translation_literal: Let them be like the grass of the roofs, that before it is drawn out it has withered.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them be like the grass that grows on the roofs: it springs up in the thin dirt, and the sun has dried it before it ever stands tall.
verses.directors_commentary:
Every listener knew the grass on a flat Near Eastern roof: roofs were of beaten clay and earth over reeds and beams, and after the winter rain a green fuzz of seedlings would come up in the thin soil, and the summer sun would burn it dry in days. It is the proverbial image of a thing that never matures (2 Kings 19:26 = Isaiah 37:27 uses the same grass). Nothing comes of it. This is the second image of the psalm, taken from the same village world as the plough, and it is a mean, small one: not a tree uprooted but a weed that never gets to be a plant.

The hard phrase is שֶׁקַּדְמַת שָׁלַף יָבֵשׁ. Rashi, Metzudat David, Metzudat Zion and Malbim take שלף as 'pull up, pluck': it is dry before anyone can pull it up. Radak, Meiri and Ibn Ezra take it as 'come out, emerge', the way a sword is drawn from its sheath: it is dry before it comes out into view. The KJV, ASV and BBE ('groweth up', 'comes to full growth') follow this second reading. The Hebrew can carry either, and both mean the same thing: it dies before use. KJV 'withereth afore it groweth up' is a fair reading. Note the Hebrew puts 'withered' as the very last word, so that the verse ends dry.

philological_notes.note: 'Grass of the roofs', the weedy growth on flat clay roofs. The same phrase is in Isaiah 37:27 and 2 Kings 19:26, where it stands for the helpless.

Usually 'draw out, pull off' (a sword, a sandal: Ruth 4:7-8). Rashi, Metzudat David, Metzudat Zion and Malbim take it as 'pulled up, plucked', with the grass torn out before it can be harvested. Radak, Meiri and Ibn Ezra take it as 'come out, emerge', drawn out of the roof like a sword from its sheath. The ambiguity is the reason to keep 'drawn out' in the literal layer.

verses.translation_literal: That has not filled his hand, a reaper, and his bosom, a binder of sheaves.
verses.translation_dramatic: It will never fill the reaper's hand. It will never fill the arms, or the folds of the robe, of the one who gathers up the sheaves.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is a quick sketch of the harvest: the reaper cuts with one hand and grips a handful of stalks, and behind him comes the binder, who gathers the cut stalks against his chest in the fold of his garment (חֵצֶן) to bind them into sheaves. The roof-grass is so thin and so scant that it cannot even fill one hand, and there is nothing for the binder to carry. The ending is as dry as the grass.

The KJV 'mower' for קוֹצֵר misleads: a mower cuts hay with a scythe, but the Hebrew reaper cuts grain with a sickle. KJV also inserts 'nor' in 'nor he that bindeth sheaves'; the Hebrew has just 'and'. Rashi says the 'bosom' is the same as in Isaiah 49:22, 'they shall bring your sons in the bosom', and Ibn Ezra sets the picture against its opposite, the one who comes home with joy carrying sheaves (Psalm 126:6), an earlier song of the same series. Staged: the empty hand, the empty fold.

philological_notes.note: 'His bosom', the fold of the garment against the chest, a carrying place. The only other uses are Isaiah 49:22 and Nehemiah 5:13 ('I shook out my lap').
One who binds sheaves, from עֹמֶר 'sheaf' (Deuteronomy 24:19: 'forgot a sheaf'). A denominative participle.

verses.translation_literal: And they have not said, those passing by, 'The blessing of YHWH [be] to you; we bless you in the name of YHWH.'
verses.translation_dramatic: And no one passing by along the road has called out the harvest greeting: 'The blessing of the LORD be on you. We bless you in the name of the LORD.'
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the last picture of the psalm, the road beside the harvest field. Travellers were expected to greet workers with a blessing, as Boaz greets his reapers in Ruth 2:4 ('The LORD be with you!') and they answer ('The LORD bless you'). Radak and Meiri cite this: the harvest of a good field is greeted with God's name. For the roof-grass nobody says it, because there is nothing there to bless, and the haters of Zion are left unblessed and unseen.

The KJV 'Neither do they which go by say' turns a flat 'and not' into 'neither', and inserts 'be' (the Hebrew has no verb in 'blessing of YHWH to you'). The first greeting is a wish, the second a performative: 'we bless you', in the Hebrew perfect, spoken as the act itself. Malbim adds that the passers-by use the first greeting in plenty and the second in drought. The psalm ends not with a curse but with an absence: the saying of God's name is held back. The audience, who have just said the name aloud in verse 4, hear what silence of it would be.

philological_notes.note: 'Those who pass by', a participle with the article. These are the travellers on the field road, who by custom greeted the workers.
A Piel perfect, 'we have blessed', used as a performative: 'we bless you'. It is the act of blessing completed in the saying. Radak sets it against Boaz's greeting.
